metadata.title: Age differences in bullying victimisation and perpetration: Evidence from cross-cultural surveys

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not analyze individual-level TIMSS/HBSC/EUKO microdata; instead, it uses aggregated country-by-age-and-gender frequencies (and TIMSS scale-score summaries) obtained from the surveys’ websites/reports. Because the analysis is based on published aggregates rather than student-level records, complex survey weights and replicate-weight procedures are not described or applied in the manuscript. The authors also do not report any PV-based achievement scaling workflow, as the outcomes are bullying victimisation/perpetration prevalence trends (and TIMSS bullying scale scores are used descriptively for trend classification). Consequently, there is no explicit weighting variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to document for an international database analysis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variables are bullying victimisation/perpetration prevalence trends derived from aggregated survey outputs (and TIMSS bullying scale-score summaries), not cognitive achievement PVs. Missing-data handling is not reported because the manuscript does not perform student-level model estimation with an imputation/deletion procedure; it classifies age trends (U/D/P/V/S) using published country-level counts and reported scale-score summaries. As a result, there is no documented missingness strategy at the individual record level.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses aggregated cross-national survey outputs for bullying victimisation (all three surveys) and bullying perpetration (HBSC and EU Kids Online). For EU Kids Online, the authors restrict the age comparisons by dropping the 9–10 year data in 2010 and using a 3-point age categorisation (11–12, 13–14, 15–16) to better match HBSC ages; for TIMSS, they use grade 4 (~10 years) and grade 8 (~14 years) and classify trends as U/S/D (no P/V). For HBSC and EUKO, age trends are categorized into U (up/linear increase), S (same/no change), D (down/linear decrease), P (peak/curvilinear highest at middle age point), or V (trough/curvilinear lowest at middle age point) based on how prevalence changes across the survey’s age points.

data.outcome_summary: This paper is a cross-cultural synthesis of age-trend patterns in bullying victimisation and perpetration using three large-scale surveys: HBSC (1993/94–2017/18; ages 11/13/15), EU Kids Online (2010 and 2018/19; ages 9–16, with 9–10 dropped for comparability), and TIMSS (2011/2015/2019; grades 4 and 8). The authors do not train machine-learning models; instead, they classify each country’s age pattern into U/D/P/V/S categories and test gender differences in trend distributions using chi-square tests in SPSS. Across HBSC and TIMSS, victimisation most often shows a downward (D) trend (e.g., HBSC: 334/504 or 66% D; TIMSS: 145/185 or 78% D), while perpetration shows more mixed patterns (HBSC: predominant P and U; EUKO: predominantly U). Cyberbullying trends are more complex, with greater variability across surveys and genders. Limitations include reliance on self-report, restricted age range (~10–16), and comparability issues across survey procedures; the study uses trends rather than exact prevalence to mitigate these biases.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is not an empirical predictive/ML study: it uses published aggregated frequencies and descriptive trend classification (U/D/P/V/S) with chi-square testing, and it does not report any ML algorithms, PV handling, missing-data imputation/deletion, or student-level weighting. Therefore, ML technique fields and main_findings rows are intentionally left empty, and the extraction focuses on the survey-based methodological approach and descriptive results.
